Manufactured Homes in Rural Counties

In rural counties—those outside any metropolitan area—12.4% of occupied homes are manufactured or mobile homes, more than double the national share of 5.1%. In the most rural U.S. counties, those excluding micropolitan areas, 14.4% of occupied homes are manufactured or mobile homes.

    Share of occupied homes that are manufactured homes. Select a range to highlight those counties; select it again to clear. Metropolitan counties are not shown.

      About the Data

      What’s shown. The share of occupied homes that residents report as a mobile home in the Census Bureau’s American Community Survey (2020–2024). The survey category does not exactly match HUD’s definition of a manufactured home, and some newer manufactured homes may be reported as single-family houses.

      Rural counties. There is no single, universal definition of a rural county used by the federal government. This map follows a definition commonly used by the U.S. Department of Agriculture: all nonmetropolitan areas are displayed unless the option to show only the most rural counties is selected, then it excludes all micropolitan areas. The Office of Management and Budget defines a metropolitan area as having an urban core of 50,000 or more people and a micropolitan area as having an urban core of 10,000 to 49,999 people. Both metropolitan and micropolitan areas include surrounding counties with strong commuting ties to the core. The rural shares above use combined totals for all counties in each group, not averages of county shares.

      Coverage. The map shows 1,958 rural counties in 48 states: 658 micropolitan counties and 1,300 of the most rural counties. New Jersey, Rhode Island, and the District of Columbia have no rural counties under this definition. When the map is limited to the most rural counties, which span 44 states, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, and Massachusetts also have none.

      Small counties. Estimates for counties with few homes can be imprecise. Each county’s pop-up shows a range likely to contain the true value.

      How this map was made. BPC staff used Anthropic’s Claude to help assemble data from the American Community Survey and OMB’s metropolitan area delineations, calculate the estimates and margins of error, and build this interactive map. BPC staff defined the measures, reviewed the methodology, and checked the results.

      Source: BPC analysis of U.S. Census Bureau, American Community Survey 2020–2024 five-year estimates, table B25032; 2024 cartographic boundary files; Office of Management and Budget metropolitan and micropolitan delineations, July 2023; rural definition from the U.S. Department of Agriculture Economic Research Service. Alaska and Hawaii are repositioned and not to scale.
